speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House has just lost one of its most eminent members, Mr. Bernard Pilon, member for Chambly since 1962 and Whip of the government party.
The House of Commons is losing not only a member of great ability and exceptional devotion but also a man who had, through his warm humanity and his generous and sympathetic personality, won the respect and the friendship of all. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that I speak for all hon. members, when I say that he will be sorely missed and that his sudden passing leaves a great void here.
To Mrs. Pilon, his family and his friends, I offer, in the name of all members of the House, our very sincere condolences.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
We have just learned, Mr. Speaker, of the untimely death of Mr. Pilon, member for Chambly and Whip of the Liberal party.
Mr. Pilon who was elected in 1962 has always been considered since, by all hon. members with whom he was acquainted, as a kindly man, who liked life and who could control his feelings and reactions. All of us, whatever our party affiliations, have always appreciated his sense of humour; we are all losing a friend.

Of Mr. Pilon, Sir, it can be truthfully said that he had the respect and admiration of all members of this House. He was a warm and affectionate man, and we will all hold fine memories of his work here.

To all his colleagues, to the members of his family as well as to his friends, I extend on behalf of my party, my sincere sympathy.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members in all parts of the House were saddened to learn only a few hours ago of the untimely death of Mr. Bernard Pilon, the member for Chambly. He entered the House in 1962, and it is a measure of the strength of his personality that he very soon became the whip of his party. In this very exacting post, one which, if occupied by a more abrasive personality, could cause a good deal of friction, Bernie, as he was commonly called, won the respect and the admiration
of all with whom he came in contact. Those of us on this side of the House came to know him as a friendly, likeable and pleasant personality. We feel saddened today by his passing and we hope that you, Sir, on behalf of the members of this House will convey to Madame Pilon our deepest sympathy at the great loss which she and the members of her family have suffered in the passing of her husband.

Mr. Speaker, as all my colleagues in the House, I was shocked when I heard the news of the sudden death of Bernard Pilon at the age of 52.
Bernard Pilon was a friend of mine. I came to know him as soon as he was elected to the House in 1962. Since then he and I have been members of parliamentary delegations in Iran and India where I had the occasion to appreciate his superb qualities.
AH will remember that Bernard was generous and amiable and that he was more of a humanitarian than a politician.
Mr. Speaker, Parliament has lost a dedicated servant. The electors of his Chambly riding have not only lost a public servant but a friend. As to the government, it is being deprived of one of the most remarkable members it has been our privilege to know.
And so on behalf of my colleagues and on my behalf, I wish to extend to Mrs. Pilon and the family our most sincere sympathy.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Prime Minister in the absence of the Minister of Finance who has expressed concern about possible protectionist tendencies in the United States and the implications of this for Canada. Is it the position of the government of Canada that the protectionist trends in the United States are contrary to GATT or any other international convention, or is it the position of the government of Canada that what is contemplated there does not contravene any international agreement but would simply be against the interests of the development of world trade and in particular of Canada's world trade?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: UNITED STATES PROTECTIONIST TRENDS-CANADIAN POSITION-CONSULTATIONS WITH EUROPEAN COMMON MARKET AUTHORITIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we will have to see how these policies develop in order to judge whether they will be contrary to the GATT or not. It is our belief that the United States will not develop policies contrary to the GATT, and of course we are expressing hope that they will not depart from the generally held belief in the benefits of multilateral trade. I had occasion to express this hope of the government of Canada to President Nixon when I first met him a year and a half ago.

subtopic: UNITED STATES PROTECTIONIST TRENDS-CANADIAN POSITION-CONSULTATIONS WITH EUROPEAN COMMON MARKET AUTHORITIES
speechtext: When the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce visited Brussels a few weeks ago, Mr. Speaker, he not only expressed concern about the consequences of protectionism which might develop in the United States but also the concern felt by Canadians that protectionism might develop in the Common Market itself. In our discussions of the possible consequences of the entry of the United Kingdom into the Common Market we reiterated these concerns. So the speech by the Minister of Finance yesterday is part of the reiteration of these very serious concerns we have with the development of world trade by the formation of blocs, whether within Europe or within the United States. It is of great importance to Canada that multilateral trade continue to be viewed by the world trading nations as the best way to proceed. We have also had discussions along these lines in Australia and New Zealand and there have been return visits here by some of their officials. We are trying to impress these views upon the world trading nations.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, without taking very much of the time of the committee, I wish to move an amendment to clause 9(l)(a) and a similar amendment to clause 9(l)(c) of Bill C-181. I could do this separately or place both amendments in your hands, Mr. Chairman, and you could put them before the committee as you see fit. I move:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext: Order. The amendments presented by the hon. member for York South deal with clause 9 and, in particular, two subclauses thereof. Unless there should be representation to the contrary, it would seem to the Chair that we might deal with these amendments together.

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not require much time in which to support the amendments I have respectfully moved. I am sure the minister is perhaps even better aware of the difference I am seeking to introduce. I say that whatever may have been the situation on October 16, at this stage the police ought not to have the power to go around arresting people on mere suspicion, without reasonable and probable grounds for that suspicion. I merely draw the attention of the minister and of the committee to a simple fact that everyone knows. If my arithmetic is correct, something like 85 per cent of the persons arrested under the regulation under the War Measures Act were released without charge and less than 10 per cent have been charged to date, unless there is later information. In addition, some others are still being kept in custody.
I suggest that at this stage of the game there is no excuse for varying the usual provisions of our criminal law. You will note, Mr. Chairman, that I am not suggesting the provision that the officer may arrest without warrant be changed. It is precisely because he may arrest without warrant that I believe it is important for the law to contain the kind of language with which a peace officer is acquainted, and which will make him look much more carefully at the situation before he goes around putting people in jail, even for seven days. A person ought not be put in jail without charge unless the police officer has probable and reasonable grounds for suspecting that such a person is a member of the unlawful association or that he has committed, is committing or is about to commit an act described in the earlier clauses of the bill. I do not think this restriction would interfere with his police work.
What this really does in practical terms is put the peace officer on guard. He will know that if he goes around arresting someone without reasonable and probable grounds, that person may go into court at some later

November 17, 1970

date and charge the policeman or police organization, whatever it may be, with false arrest and seek a remedy against such false arrest. I submit that at this stage of the situation in the province of Quebec this added protection for people who might be arrested ought to be in the bill.
In conclusion, I want to say I do not think this would reduce the peace officer's power in any reasonable way. He would still be able to arrest without warrant, but instead of being able to arrest on a subjective conclusion of his own that he has reason to suspect, he would have to have an objective reason for it. He would have to analyse the situation and have some prima facie evidence that would lead him and that would lead a court or any reasonable tribunal to conclude that the arrest was made on probable and reasonable grounds. That is the only distinction. I suggest it is a very important distinction in order to avoid the situation we have had, where 440 or so people were arrested and 390 of them released without being charged. This means that 85 per cent or 90 per cent of these people, or at least most of them, obviously were arrested without probable or reasonable grounds for the suspicion the police officer had. This has been done within recent weeks, particularly during the critical situation that was said to exist on October 16. The committee knows my view concerning what the situation really was, but the critical situation was said to exist on October 16. It is important that from now on the police forces in Quebec, acting under this law whenever it comes into effect, have probable and reasonable grounds for arresting someone under suspicion for the acts dealt with in clause 9 of the bill.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman.
Public Order Act, 1970
The amendment proposed by the hon. member for York South would change subclause 3 as follows, if I seize the purport of his amendment. It would read: "a peace officer may arrest without warrant a person who he has reasonable and probable grounds to suspect is a member of the unlawful association". I want to say to him that the words we chose, namely the words "reason to suspect" were deliberately chosen. As I pointed out in my speech on second reading, particularly as recorded at page 883 of Hansard, clause 9 is a special measure which the government recognizes does not exist in the ordinary criminal law.
We are dealing with specific short term legislation to meet a specific purpose, namely to attempt to immobilize and render inefficient the FLQ. The requirement "to have reason to suspect" is less stringent than that contained in the Criminal Code which requires the existence of reasonable and probable grounds to believe that an indictable offence has been committed. I refer hon. members to section 435(a) of the Criminal Code. The amendment does not remove the word "suspect" in clause 9(l)(a), and I assume this was done deliberately. However, by doing it deliberately, the hon. member leaves us with a hybrid concept, neither "reason to suspect" nor "reasonable and probable grounds to believe", but "reasonable and probable grounds to suspect", I believe this would confuse the case law even more than it may be confused already as to what the words "reasonable and probable grounds" may mean.
In any event, the amendment is obviously designed to make the condition precedent to lawful arrest more stringent, and in the present circumstances the government does not favour that. We are of the view that the requirement "reason to suspect" is both necessary and reasonable in the circumstances. It is the equivalent of the requirement prescribed in the statutes, principally with regard to matters of national security. I refer to the Official Secrets Act. Section 10 of the act provides:
Every person who is found committing an offence under this Act, or who is reasonably suspected of having committed, or having attempted to commit, or being about to commit, such an offence, may be arrested without a warrant and detained by any constable or police officer.
I want to submit to the committee that hon. members should not be under any apprehension that the words "reason to suspect" means that a person can be arrested without grounds. In order to satisfy the requirement in clause 9 (1) (a) as it is now written, there must be a bona fide reason to suspect that a person is a member of the illegal or unlawful association. In the absence of any bona fide reason to suspect, the provision would not apply. subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISION OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the main purpose I am trying to achieve-and I had hoped the minister might look upon it a little more reasonably than he seems to do-is to remove from the police the temptation to wholesale arrest, as has happened since October 16. I do not see how any Member of Parliament or how the Minister of Justice can look with equanimity at a situation where 450 people are arrested, all of them held in jail and 397 of them released without charge after being in jail for six days, 10 days, 12 days or 21 days. I do not understand how anyone in Canada can look with equanimity at a situation where 90 per cent of the persons arrested are released without charge after being kept in jail, sometimes incommunicado.
I submit that all I am trying to achieve is to let the police know that they must have reasonable and probable grounds even for suspicion, even if it is something less than belief. To say that they must have reasonable and probable grounds for believing would be too much in the present instance, and on that I agree with the minister. However, their suspicion must be based on some reasonable ground. I am not a police officer nor am I an intelligence officer so I cannot tell you what the grounds might be, but as a layman I can see a situation where an officer may have interviewed the 450 people who have been arrested-it may be 460 before the bill becomes law-and as a result of his conversations he has reasonable ground to believe that X or Y was or is a member of the FLQ. This would be reasonable or probable ground for that suspicion. I want to prevent the continuation of the situation which I think is scandalous and unforgivable. It is a kind of excessive zeal on the part of the police which a democratic society should not tolerate.
Perhaps there is an indication of incompetence when 450 people are arrested, with all the consequences that flow from arrest, not only being kept in jail incommunicado but being under the cloud of having been arrested in connection with the FLQ and then released. As I said the other day, I have met some of them. They told me they cannot explain to their children why they were in jail. To my knowledge, two of them lost their jobs. Arrest has consequences; it is not a picnic, it is not a tea party, and when 400 out of 450 people are arrested apparently without grounds because they were released without charge, then I think the situation is very serious. The purpose of my amendment is not so much to affect the end result in the court-one can never foretell that- but to achieve a desirable influence on the police so that they would be less likely to go around picking up anyone about whom they may have a suspicion.

I say to the minister that I am quite ready to suggest to him that I drop the adjective "probable" and leave the words "reasonable grounds". In my submission, the difference between saying that the fellow has reason to suspect and saying he has reasonable grounds to suspect is quite obvious. In the one case it is a subjective reaction. I have reason to suspect, so I make an arrest. In the other case it is an objective test that there has to be a ground for his suspicion that can be looked at objectively by anyone, including a tribunal. The reason for the amendment is to stop the wholesale, scandalous, excessive, incompetent type of arrest which obviously has taken place since October 16.
# (3:20 p.m.)
I repeat that I, as one Canadian, as one member of this parliament, simply cannot tolerate the arrest of 450 people, 400 of whom are released after some days in jail without any charge against them. These people have to carry all the consequences of having been arrested, having been associated with the FLQ when obviously they were not or they would have been charged. They have had to undergo the shame, the humiliation, the inconvenience and the discomfiture of having been jailbirds for six, eight, ten or 21 days without any charge, and without any grounds for their arrest.
If you had the qualification which I suggest should be placed in the bill, then the police officers would be a great deal more careful. They would follow not quite the procedure they follow in ordinary crime because they don't have to believe that a person may be guilty, they have only to suspect he may be, but they would be put on guard that they must have reasonable or probable grounds for that suspicion or else face the possibility later of being dragged into court on a civil suit for damages for false arrest.

The minister says that in order to effect the apprehension of those in the FLQ who are committed to terrorist activities we need this kind of legislation, even though he still fails to define the exact nature of the illegal organization. It is in no way indicative of any kind of objective information or facts that are normally required for due process of apprehension and arrest. It is completely left to the subjective opinion and feelings of the individual police officer.
I would argue that "reason to suspect" means nothing more than how the individual police officer may feel when he comes up to any specific individual. If he gets up in the morning after a poor night, tired and irritable, and he runs into somebody he does not like, under this phrase "reason to suspect" he can place that person under arrest. That is the sum total of what "reason to suspect" means. It has nothing to do with the facts that need to be available for proper arrest. The reason may be good, bad or indifferent. The clause just stipulates "reason to suspect." If the minister is seriously interested in the cause of justice, he will move immediately to accept the amendment.
The minister tells us that we are dealing with a special situation and with short-term legislation. We, in turn, also know that we are dealing with a very serious situation in the province of Quebec which has raised fundamental questions about the effectiveness of the whole police organization. Hon. members and people throughout the country have been wondering about the inefficiency of the police, and about the adequacy of their judgment. How in the name of all that is just and right could the minister be arguing for these kinds of broad, subjective powers to be placed in the hands of a police organization, which, on a number of counts during the past few weeks, has proved itself woefully short of good judgment?

Mr. Chairman, may 1 say first that I am not wedded to that particular language. If the minister were prepared to accept the idea, 1 and my colleagues would be prepared to have him produce something satisfactory.
The point of this amendment is sharpened by what has happened, to which reference has been made a number of times. We have to look at the facts since October 16 as far as we know them, and the facts relevant to this amendment are the following: First, some 450 people have been arrested but some 397 of them were released as of ten o'clock this morning, I think the minister said; second, for some days many of them-perhaps all of them-were kept incommunicado without being given access to counsel. This is now public knowledge. I am not saying this happened in every case because I do not know, but I am not saying this happened in every case because I do not know, but I am saying that it probably happened in every case and that it certainly happened in most cases. These people who were arrested were kept incommunicado for many days without being given the opportunity to see and retain counsel, without being given the opportunity to see their wives or members of

November 17, 1970

their families, or indeed to communicate with them in any way whatsoever in the first week or so.
Later, after the first six or seven days, in some cases that have come to my attention, those in jail were given the right to write a note to their wives. In the cases that have come to my attention the people involved were wives. They were given the opportunity to write a note to their wives, and a policeman or guard at the jail, then read the note over the telephone to the incarcerated person's wife. They were not allowed, in the cases that have come to my attention and this is not guesswork as I have spoken with 10 or 12 of these people, some of whom were in my office, to have their textbooks. Students, one of them from Carleton University and the other from the University of Ottawa, were not allowed to have their textbooks during the time they were incarcerated, although they pleaded for them because they wanted to continue their work. In one case that has come to my attention a wife brought some clothing for her husband who was arrested and he got the clothing after he left the jail. He was in jail eight days and had no change of underwear or shirt or any other piece of clothing and was released without charge but was in.erv.ewed for only ten minutes during those eight days. I cannot tell you how many times this kind of thing occurred, but the fact is these things have happened since October 16, and as sure as you and I are here they will happen again if things are left as they are.
It was interesting to read the report of the Civil Liberties Association of Montreal. It was a report prepared by Mr. Hebert and his committee of three who not only complained about the conditions under which people were being kept under arrest but also cynically pointed out that for some reason they were given a date to visit jails at a time when most of the people who were in jail had already been released. This is the kind of thing he found and reported to the press. I have read the reports and could quote them if I wanted to take the time or if anyone here has not read them. I listened to Mr. Hebert at one time on ihe television, both in English and in French, when he gave a description of what he found.
The minister is going to say again, I have no doubt, as he has said throughout, this is an extraordinary piece of legislation to deal with an extraordinary set of circumstances and to break up an extraordinary terrorist organization. If he is right in all of these things, and I know he is right in at least some of them, then I think the situation requires extraordinary remedies and extraordinary safeguards.
If he refuses, as he has done before, to accept efforts to lessen the arbitrariness and repressiveness of the bill which is before us, then he ought to agree to this suggestion of appointing a supervising commission of three independent people who will make sure that those who are arrested on mere suspicion and kept in jail up to seven days, instead of the longer period under the regulation, are treated according to law and according to a sense of decency and of justice which even our worst criminals get in normal times.

I therefore say to him that precisely because this is extraordinary legislation, and precisely because it is legislation that abridges very seriously a good many normal liberties and rights, this kind of supervisory body should be established. In an amendment which I have seen which the official opposition intends to move an administrator is suggested, although personally I prefer the notion of a commission of three rather than one person. Such a body should be established to provide a safeguard against abuse, against over-zealousness, against arbitrariness and against incompetence. Such a provision should be put into the law because since October 16 we have had experience with all these things, arbitrariness, abuse and incompetence. There is only one way to make sure that will not happen again; that is, by establishing through this piece of extraordinary legislation a special kind of supervisory commission to make sure that those persons arrested are treated properly.
The reason for subclause (b) in the amendment is that I want to be sure, as I assume the minister himself would want to be sure, the new commission would operate under conditions which would ensure that its findings become public so that the people of Canada would know exactly what was happening, since the only final sanction against abuse of the type I have described is the anger and annoyance of the people of Canada or the people of the province of Quebec as the case may be. I do not intend to say anything more now, Mr. Chairman. The evidence of what has happened in the last few weeks makes clear that such a provision is necessary and that such a supervisory commission is desirable. Unless the minister can show very good cause why this provision should not be incorporated in the bill I invite him to accept it. If he does not like my language, but accepts the idea, then we can see his language or the language of his officers because I do not suppose it would be his.

Mr. Chairman, in asking parliament to adopt this bill the Minister of Justice, on behalf of the government, is asking the people of Canada to adopt the kinds of controls to which we have never agreed in peacetime in the history of Canada. Part and parcel of this bill is the right to search, the right to arrest without warrant and the right to hold people without permitting
Public Order Act, 1970
them to contact their families or counsel. We, in our party, have been criticized because we voted in support of this bill on second reading. We did so because we felt that this was a lesser evil than the War Measures Act and because we thought that the minister, in the light of his statements and expressions of the past couple of years which tended to show, as my colleague for Calgary North suggested, that the minister was a progressive sort of person, would accept reasonable amendments. Mr. Chairman, the longer this debate continues the more it becomes obvious that we were wrong in our judgment. By refusing to approve any and every amendment, the Minister of Justice is asking parliament to approve a bill which lays down the stringent conditions I have enumerated very briefly. And, not being satisfied with that, Mr. Chairman, the minister suggests that the federal government and Parliament should thereafter wash their hands of the bill and permit the attorney general of one province to administer it.
When the amendment proposing an independent review committee was brought in, the Minister of Justice tried to argue that the amendment was not necessary because the Attorney General of Quebec had already agreed to the establishment of a committee which, according to the Minister of Justice, had the powers which this amendment would give to such a committee. Actually, that committee has no power under the law. That committee can only do those things which the Attorney General of Quebec permits it to do. The Attorney General of Quebec can pay to it as much or as little attention as he chooses.

subtopic: PUBLIC ORDER (TEMPORARY MEASURES) ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS OF EMERGENCY POWERS FOR PRESERVATION OF PUBLIC ORDER
speechtext: That is right.

speechtext:
I will not go into the record of the operations of the present government of Quebec under the provisions of the War Measures Act. I say to the Minister of Justice that if he is not disturbed about some of the proposals which have been made by the Attorney General of Quebec, he is possibly the only so-called Liberal in this country who is not disturbed.
Let us look at the speeches and statements which the Attorney General of Quebec has been making. He has proposed that every citizen of Quebec be required to carry an identity card. I presume that means photographing and fingerprinting and everything else that goes towards making up a real identity card. He has implied that the freedom of the press may need to be restricted. He has also implied that the fundamental and traditional freedoms which citizens of Canada have enjoyed ever since there has been a country may have to be restricted.
I for one, Mr. Chairman, am not prepared to vote for a bill which would give some other person, the Attorney General of Quebec, the right to restrict the rights of citizens in Quebec in the way in which the present Attorney General of Quebec has indicated. The Minister of Justice may have a very short memory; I suggest that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion ought to have better memories. This is not the first time the people of Canada and the people of Quebec have had to deal with attorneys general who thought that there were reasons-good reasons so far as

November 17, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
they were concerned-tor restricting the rights of the citizens of their province. I remind the members of the committee and the Minister of Justice that the former premier of Quebec, Mr. Duplessis, was also the attorney general of Quebec. Under his regime we had the padlock law in Quebec. Under his regime in Quebec the asbestos strike was smashed, with the use of police, in a bloody way. Under his regime we had the strike at the Gaspe copper mines in which the present Prime Minister was involved.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
We have had varying experiences with the attorneys general of Quebec. I am only talking about Quebec because this bill will have effect, at present at least, only in Quebec. When Mr. Duplessis was carrying on as he did, when Mr. Duplessis was passing the padlock law, he had virtually the unanimous approval of the press and of the legislature of that province. As I say he enjoyed, virtually, the unanimous approval of the press and the approval, or at least their acquiescence through silence, of the Members of Parliament from Quebec. We, who are not in Quebec, are being told not to pay any attention to all these things. I wonder if the Prime Minister would change his views about the kind of regime they had in Quebec when Mr. Duplessis was premier? I wonder whether the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, who lived through the days when these things were taking place in the province of Quebec, has forgotten what Mr. Duplessis did? Have they asked themselves what Mr. Duplessis could have done in that province had there been the legislation that is being proposed today?

I will then be happy to hear from the Parliamentary Secretary or the hon. member if they would like to defend Mr. Duplessis. The Parliamentary Secretary shakes his head. I say to him that the legislation being proposed today is foursquare with what Mr. Duplessis did during his time. Because I feel this way, I have no intention of voting for this bill.
The Minister of Justice will not accept any amendment which calls on the Attorney General of Quebec, or any other province which may have to use this legislation, to keep in mind the democratic rights of their citizens. The Minister of Justice has shed the liberal views which he expressed so often with regard to bail and the right to counsel. I do not agree with terrorists and separatism, but people have a right to say what they think. They do not have the right to kidnap people, kill them or plant bombs, but in this country they have the right to say what they think. This bill will help certain groups in Quebec which do not believe that people have this right and want to put the clamps on them. I do not support that feeling.
I wish to record some thoughts of a man who is much more eloquent than I, although unfortunately he seems to have changed his views. I wish to read some views which he held before entering politics. I will quote from the November 14, 1970 issue of the Winnipeg Free Press. It contains a summary of a book which will be published shortly by the Oxford University Press. The name of the book is "Approaches to Politics". By whom was the book written? It was written by our Prime Minister, Pierre Elliott Trudeau. I am quoting for the benefit of the members from Quebec and the Liberal backbenchers who feel certain that what now is being done is right and necessary, namely abridging the freedoms of their people:
Democracy recognizes that one person may be right and ninety-nine wrong; that is why freedom of speech is sacred. The one person must always have the right to proclaim his truth in the hope of persuading the ninety-nine to change their point of view-
One can say that the power of government rests on a psychological disposition on most people's part that it is good to obey and bad to disobey. Why is this belief so universal? Partly because the majority seek only their own comfort and pleasure: When those ends are assured, they ask no more than to conform to a given social order and to obey political masters who work to maintain that order. Few men are aroused by injustice when they are sure of not being its victims themselves.
If that is not a classic illustration of what is going on in Quebec today, and how the government of Quebec is dealing with the situation, I have not heard of one. I wish to read another short paragraph:
Citizens must take care to delegate to (the state) no more authority, no more force, than are strictly necessary to establish a just social order, protect that order from harm, and make sure it will progress.
I suggest that the government is not heeding these words of the Prime Minister because they are giving the government of Quebec a great deal more power than is necessary or wise.

By giving the Quebec Minister of Justice the right to file a certificate, we are giving him the right to decide whether there is just cause for detaining a person in jail, over and above the usual causes. These powers far exceed those he inherited when he took office, and in these circumstances responsibility lies upon us to make sure there is accountability for the exercise of these powers. We recognize that certain individuals are invested with authority by the people of a province; there are those who exercise authority as members of a cabinet. This is a situation we accept. But we are now being asked to delegate extraordinary powers which do not normally fall within the ambit of any member of an elected government, powers usually exercised only by judges who are appointed for life and who have a special responsibility to sit in judgment upon their fellows.

We are not concerned at this moment with whether a person, be he the Minister of Justice for Quebec or the Minister of Justice for Canada, is to be trusted or not. It seems to me the lawyers among us are beginning to clear away some of the haze. What is happening is beginning to stir their consciences as members of the bar trained in the law with a duty to seek justice not only for those who are innocent but also for those who are guilty.
It is time for us to assess what we are being asked to do. We supported the invocation of the War Measures Act and its regulations on the understanding that legislation would be introduced to meet the particular circumstances. In so doing, we had expected the government would show a reasonable attitude toward proposals and ideas which would be advanced from this side of the chamber so as to produce legislation which would truly reflect the wishes of this grand body. It seems to me that what we have been witnessing has been an exercise in frustration. Surely the minister realizes that the extra powers we are asked to confer are of such a nature that abuse could arise because of human frailty, yet for some reason he is reluctant to move in this area of law reform, though it is precisely his interest in this field which I have admired in him as he goes across the country speaking. Apparently he is not prepared to accept safeguards, and I find this attitude wholly unrealistic, wholly inconsistent with what he is preaching in the land. I cannot understand it. I do not doubt that this legislation is needed. But in its present form it is loaded to an unprecedented degree in favour of peace officers, in favour of the Crown, in favour of the Attorney General and in favour of the Government of Canada.
It has been said that with the invocation of the War Measures Act, Canada will never be the same again. I hope we have not reached a point at which, in attempting to protect the innocent, we have not forgotten about their rights entirely. Someone has to be the conscience of the government if we are to be consistent with the new thinking of the Minister of Justice, if we are to be consistent with our democratic way of life, if we are to be true to our democratic institutions. It is all very well for the minister to say that his responsibility ends with the proclamation of this measure and that its administration can be left to someone else. We are told this is a bad amendment because by-adopting it we would write into a future statute a restriction on a provincial attorney general. Surely, since it is a federal statute we are being asked to vote upon and endorse, we have the right to do that. Surely it would not be too much to ask the Minister of Justice to say to the Attorney General of Quebec, "If you want this kind of legislation and if you need it, we are prepared to bring it in; but we think you ought to have this kind of committee.'' This would not be a committee set up by some kind of verbal or written order on the part of the minister, which he could revoke tomorrow, next year or whenever it suits him, or the moment the committee starts being critical of him. Surely the Minister of Justice should say to the Attorney General of Quebec, "If you want this legislation you must write into your statutes the provision that there will be an independent committee."
I do not think we would quarrel about the three people who might be appointed. Certainly we would not quarrel about the appointment of Mr. Hebert. I would be prepared to accept the view of the Attorney General of Quebec and the Minister of Justice that it was a good committee. But let us have written into the law of the province that wants to use this legislation which we as Members of Parliament are being asked to approve that there will be an independent committee. Then if people's rights are infringed, if they are held too long and are not permitted counsel, talk to their families or have books and newspapers to read, the committee will have the power to do something other than just plead with the Attorney General of the province.
We are told that this committee might take the place of the courts, but that is not true and the members who put forward that argument must know it is not true. We are concerned that this bill takes from the courts the traditional rights the courts have always had. A lawyer representing an accused who is being held can go to the courts, as they did in Montreal last week, with a writ of habeas corpus asking the judge to protect the rights of the person involved. After listening to argument on behalf of the Crown and the defence, the court can decide whether the person ought to be released on bail. We are not questioning the right of the courts to do that; we are saying that this bill sets down conditions under which the courts will not be able to fulfil the judicial function they have had since the beginning of this coun-

I say that until now, we have treated this as a serious, emergency matter. The fact that a man I knew in Halifax, Mr. Cross, is still held somewhere in the province of Quebec by terrorists, and is held successfully despite tremendous police and armed forces searches, to me indicates we are dealing with a conspiracy that is not the fly-by-night work of amateurs but the work of experienced, skilled and resourceful persons. I have had that thought very much in mind throughout this whole debate, even though sometimes it is pretty hard to believe it is a serious matter when we do not see the galleries filled with people, or when the Prime Minister of this country is away from the House so much during what we are told is a period of tremendous national crisis. I can accept those things, however, because I knew Mr. Cross and I know he is still held somewhere against his will and is being used as a pawn in a very dangerous game in which all Canadians have a stake.
These are the questions which have prompted many of my colleagues and myself to become involved in this somewhat drawn-out debate. It has been drawn out much beyond the time we expected. Last Friday, for example, I believe the official opposition took up five or seven minutes to deal with points which we knew had not been dealt with already. We were not inclined to take up the time of the committee. But, sir, when we have a point we can dig in our heels as well as others. This heel-digging is on the matter of the awesome powers to be granted the Attorney General of the province of Quebec.
In effect, the government of Quebec has come to Ottawa and asked that we provide an extraordinary

police force for use in that province. The whole tenor of this legislation is that the administration of law and order in the province of Quebec is to be beefed up by an almost superhuman pouring in of resources from all parts of Canada. We have been good enough to give the Attorney General and the Premier of Quebec those powers and those resources without quibbling. No one has said the army or that extra Royal Canadian Mounted Police should not be there. As a matter of fact, the reverse has been the case. I recall the leader of the New Democratic Party a few days ago asking whether the RCMP had been withdrawn. He was told they had not been withdrawn.
We do not mind the federal government or the provinces coming in to help the authorities in Quebec during a critical period. No one has quarrelled about this at all. But there must be limits. The Minister of Justice himself imposed one limit when he did not invoke the regulations of the War Measures Act for ever and a day and when he did not word this legislation in such a way that it would be in effect for ever and a day. There is an expiry date in this legislation. I think that is a fair inference to be drawn from what has gone on; otherwise why that time limit was imposed, would be incomprehensible to any sensible mind.
We are dealing with ideologies of a terrorist movement. This movement will not come to an end by the time this legislation expires next April. The point I want to make is a political one. If we are seriously concerned about what may be called the civilized and democratic leadership in the province of Quebec, we as the federal Parliament have a very important obligation to create a body that would supervise the implementation of these extraordinary new powers being bestowed upon the Attorney General and the police forces of Quebec. I say this because it is what I call the civilized and democratic leading element in the province of Quebec that has been most vocal in its criticism of the federal government, and it is mainly this group of French Canadians in the province of Quebec that should concern us very much. It is they who are pointing the finger at Ottawa and saying, "There are your centralizers, your authoritarians. It is Ottawa that is taking away French Canadian freedoms in general". I plead with the Minister of Justice to stand by the statement of the Prime Minister, that he counts on the legislative record of this Parliament in the field of individual liberties. I call on him to stand by his own words, that he wants to get back to the continuing enhancement and protection of civil liberties as soon as possible. To suggest that we cannot do so because of some jurisdictional difficulty is to talk, in my opinion, utter irrelevancy. It is our duty in this Parliament to make this law as good as it is possible to make it. What does this mean in terms of this particular bill?

Mr. Chairman, I cannot disguise the fact that I am very impressed by the eloquence to which I have been subjected during the past three or four hours, and that I have been impressed by the sources of that eloquence. operating out of Quebec. The purpose was to mobilize only those extensions in power for the law enforcement authorities that in our opinion were needed, namely, specific extensions of the power to arrest without warrant, to detain before a charge was laid for a specific period of time, to search without warrant and the other powers that have already been described in detail to this committee during clause by clause review of the bill.
We have been conscious of the fact that we had to draft and cast those powers in terms that did not go beyond the scope needed to meet the threat. We were also conscious of the fact that we did not want to interfere with the ordinary liberties of Canadians as they have been built up through the traditions of our country, whether at common law or by statute, any more than they had to be interfered with. I have tried to meet every argument that has been broached on the floor of this chamber since debate on clause by clause began; I have tried to meet it with counter argument which may or may not have been persuasive in so far as the total membership of this committee is concerned. In any event, I have tried my best to outline the government's position.
I want to assure the committee that before this debate began and during the course of the debate we have tried to assess, and I personally have tried to assay,i the value of each argument supporting each amendment. In the final analysis the government will have to bear the responsibility of the action we are taking, and we understand that. We also recognize that what we did depends in the long run on a value judgment which only history will verify or rebut, and there being no certainty in human affairs there is no one here who can fully determine what the final accounting or verdict will be. But we did what we did because we felt it had to be done. We used the vehicle and the tool of the bill before the committee because we thought that it struck the proper balance between extension of the power of law enforcement agencies on the one hand and restriction of individual liberties of Canadians to the minimum necessary to achieve its objective on the other hand.
I have considered the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Calgary North; he introduced it with verve and eloquence tonight. But I must reject it and recommend to the committee that it be rejected for basically two reasons. First, it offends against the principle, under our federal structure as it operates at the moment, in law enforcement, that the administration of justice under the Criminal Code and under those measures akin to the Criminal Code is the responsibility of the Attorneys General of the provinces. Just as the amendment introduced by the hon. member for York South implied a supervision of the discretion inherent in the responsibilities of a provincial Attorney General, so the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Calgary North has, to my mind, the same objective. It is he, the Attorney General who is responsible to the people of Quebec, to the legislature of Quebec, who must bear the ultimate accounting for how this will be administered, just as I, within the general content of this bill and of the criminal law, have to bear responsibility for that-

That brings me to my second ground for objecting and it is this: I believe in responsible government. I believe that under the British parliamentary system, the person charged with the institution of criminal proceedings, the person charged with exercising that sometimes awesome discretion and the person who under the terms of this bill has the discretion either to suspend bail or not, either to detain a person or not to detain him, or to institute prosecution or not, must be someone responsible directly to the people. All that is his responsibility under the Constitution as it operates in this country. He has to exercise that responsibility in weighing what the public interest will be. He has to weigh that public interest, not for political motivation-indeed, under our tradition, which binds Quebec as it does the federal government, he cannot institute or withhold proceedings on the basis of that consideration-but in the best interests of the administration of justice. That is his responsibility, as it is mine within the sphere within which I am appointed to operate.
The Attorney General of any province, accountable as he is to the legislature, accountable as he is through the legislature to the people, must be more sensitive to the administration or to the possibility of the maladministration of justice than any commission responsible to no one. I do not think that any paraphernalia or any superstructure of review can in any way derogate from the fundamental responsibility of an Attorney General under the British parliamentary system. There is no way in which that can be done.
When I read the third paragraph, in particular, of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Calgary North, when I see that the administrator who would enjoy judicial office, holding judicial office, would be given the power to review and "confirm, vary or revoke a certificate filed by an Attorney General of a province under subsection (1) of section 7"-that is the clause in the bill relating to the granting or withholding of bail-I do not believe that a judge should be given that responsibility or held accountable for that responsibility of an Attorney General of a province, given to him under the biU.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday, November 12, as reported at page 1090 of Hansard, I put the following question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau):
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. In view of the right hon. gentleman's statement a short while ago that he thought old age pensioners might be able to get

November 17, 1970

through the winter without an increase in their pensions, but that he hoped they would not have to, can he now say whether there will be an increase in the old age pension before Christmas?
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
The first reply of the Prime Minister was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, without agreeing with the premise of the question, which is not exactly in the terms I put it, I can only say what the Minister of National Health and Welfare has been saying, namely, that in due course he will announce the government's policy on these matters.
I tried again, by way of a supplementary, to obtain some assurance that something would at least be started before Christmas but I am afraid I was not successful. I asked the same question in different words on Monday, November 16, as recorded in Hansard at page 1188, when I put it this way:
Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister? There being 39 days to Christmas, has the Prime Minister yet decided in what way he is going to say "Merry Christmas" to Canada's old age pensioners?

maintopic: PENSIONS-OLD AGE SECURITY-ACTION ON INCREASE BEFORE CHRISTMAS
speechtext: Ho, ho, ho!

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: PENSIONS-OLD AGE SECURITY-ACTION ON INCREASE BEFORE CHRISTMAS
speechtext:
I got no answer to that so far as Hansard indicates, but I believe a number of hon. members did say what 1 have just heard-"Ho, ho, ho!"
Mr. Speaker, I apologize to the Prime Minister if he felt that my reference to what he said was not exactly correct. He did not quarrel with the general terms of my quotation but relied on the fact that I had paraphrased him a bit. Actually, I did paraphrase him by making his words softer than the press had reported. Following an interview with him outside this chamber on Friday, October 9, the press had reported the Prime Minister as saying he thought pensioners could get through the winter-I changed "could" to "might"-but it would be too bad if they had to, and he hoped it would not be necessary. I have seen reports of this interview in papers like the Ottawa Citizen of Saturday, October 10, and the Winnipeg Free Press of Monday, October 12. At any rate, it was clear that the message of the Prime Minister was one which had the effect of giving old age pensioners some hope. The headline of the story in the Ottawa Citizen was, "More Dollars for Aged". The headline of the same story in the Winnipeg Free Press was, "Pensioners Promised Action".
I think this is most unfair. It has all the earmarks of a cruel hoax for the Prime Minister to say these things and give the impression that something is going to be done, yet continue to stall in this House to the point at which it will become legislatively impossible to deal with the matter before Christmas. After all, the old age pension cheques for the month of November are probably made up already and before long the December cheques will be in production. If anything is to be done before Christmas, it must be done right away.
I remind hon. members that the situation respecting our senior citizens is getting worse and worse. The difficulties they face, in getting by on the amount they have, whether by way of pension or other income, are increasing day by day and week by week. Figures which
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion were given in answer to a question of mine some days ago, figures which are to be found in Hansard, show that 27 per cent of the people of Canada who are 65 years of age and over qualify for the full amount of the guaranteed income supplement.
In order to qualify for the full amount of that supplement one has to have practically nothing else at all. I am not now talking about the 57 per cent who qualify for some part of the guaranteed income supplement and thus are living below the poverty line. I am saying that 27 per cent of all the people in Canada 65 years of age and over are in the position that apart from what they get by way of old age pension and guaranteed income supplement they have nothing else. That means they have to get by on $111 and some cents a month. That means they are destitute.
In these days, in light of today's cost of living and in light of today's standard of living, which may be very nice for those who enjoy its affluence but which is repressive for those who cannot enjoy any part of it, I suggest this is criminal and immoral and that Parliament ought to be given the chance by the government to act on the matter of a substantial pension increase right away, certainly before Christmas.

BROADCASTING-PERFORMANCE OF NORTH BATTLEFORD SATELLITE TELEVISION STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day I asked whether the government would enforce standards required for licencing of TV stations. I had reference to the satellite in respect of North Bat-tleford through station CKBI-TV at Prince Albert.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I should like to refer briefly to a telegram I received from some of my constituents. They say that there is unbelievably poor TV reception in the Battlefords despite thousands of names on petitions sent to the TV broadcasting commission. On this telegram there are 79 names. This is not the first time the people in this area have tried to do something about the problem. The board of trade in North Battleford and many citizens on their own have attempted to have some action taken.
I asked a question on the Order Paper on November 24, 1969. These are some of the things we have done in an effort to get the attention of the minister in respect of the unbelievably poor television reception. I had assumed that when a station received a licence to broadcast it would be forced to live up to certain minimum standards. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, how you would explain the situation to your constituents or perhaps to your grandchildren if you had only one TV picture, if there was a hockey game on between Toronto and Montreal and if during the last period the score was tied and Montreal were advancing on the Toronto goal and then the picture faded out.
This is the type of thing that happens. I have heard about these things from many people, and not always in polite terms. I believe it is high time something was done about this situation. I do not want to hear excuses from the other side concerning what is wrong. I want to hear what is to be done to make the situation right. We have a TV signal that comes and goes like a yo-yo. I do not think this is necessary. If something cannot be done about this, let us give the licence to somebody else so

that we will have at least one good TV signal in North Battleford. In Ottawa, for instance, there might be eight or ten channels including three French channels. The rest of the country is talking about two channels, and we cannot even get one in our part of the country. I suggest it is time something was done to correct this problem.

GRAIN-PRODUCTION AND RECEIPTS POLICY-FARM CONSOLIDATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 29 the minister in charge of the Wheat Board tabled a program of proposals respecting the western grain industry. While the proposals are vague in many areas, one fact emanates abundantly clearly. That fact is that the contents of the new plan are based to large degree upon the task force report which outlines the Liberal government's agricultural policy platform for the seventies. This report is documented by a group of professors and accountants.
The grains program basically outlines three objectives. First, a program of supply management which could more appropriately be referred to as bureaucratic production control encompassing new marketing methods and new quota programs. It also outlines an objective of providing an income stabilization program which would be basically financed by the producers themselves. Another proposal involves an announcement that the government intends to withdraw support in the area of storage, that is, the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act, certain interest costs on export sales and the provisions covering any shortfall incurred in pool accounts. All of these collectively will reduce the net income to the producer and place the vagaries of the international marketplace squarely on the shoulders of the producer.
Above all, while achieving these goals it is suggested another development will occur and it is also included in the proposal. However, I must say that there is very little
November 17, 1970

accompanying background information and direction in this area. I am referring to the suggested proposal to encourage the adjustment of farm units into more efficient sizes. I believe that this is where more information is required.
It is for that purpose that I rise in this debate tonight. I raised the matter on November 9 and November 16. One answer that I received from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) was that the problem I raised was much too broad to be covered and dealt with in the question period. I raised the matter again yesterday in an attempt to elicit more information with respect to the government's direction and policy in this area, and inquired specifically whether a policy would be announced before the convening of the agricultural congress. To that question I received a negative answer.
The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board said that it was his desire to have the proposals thoroughly aired before proceeding with the legislation. He envisaged a debate involving the producers, the farm groups, members of the grain trades and anyone else interested in the grain industry. Yet the government's position respecting the consolidation and laying out of its intended procedure in this area have not been clearly defined. It seems to me that with such encompassing proposals, which strike at the potential disbanding of existing farm units, I as a Member of Parliament have the prerogative to ask how we can ever discuss this policy with any degree of intelligence and skill without having all the pertinent facts and without knowing the intentions of the government.
The task force report put forth some very direct proposals respecting farm adjustment and rationalization. I would simply like to ask the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, if we are to assume that the government will be following along the lines proposed in the task force report. Then we get back to the age-old question about what constitutes an economic, viable unit, what size it will have to be and whether it is the intention to doom the family farm to extinction only to have it replaced by a few corporate structures, probably vertically integrated conglomerates.
One has only to analyse the intentions of Bill C-175 and Bill C-176 and examine some of the evidence that was tabled in the committee on agriculture to conclude that it seems very obvious the government is moving in this direction. It seems to me that the government is set on a deliberate course of destroying rural Prairie life as we now know it, and in its stride bringing about the destruction of our rural communities. I believe the Canadian Economic Council on rural development also
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion bears out this fact. The saddest aspect of all is that through government measures people are being literally coerced into making undesired adjustments, with little or no recourse in so far as their options or alternatives are concerned.
If we are simply being asked to propose and agree to the policies and programs which are being brought forth in the name of efficiency, such as those contained in the task force report, the grains policy and the various bills-

Mr. Speaker, I have only three minutes and so I must be very brief in my replies to all the matters raised by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). First of all, I want to say categorically that the task force report, both in its findings and recommendations, does not constitute government policy. I think it is a great disservice to the task force, and indeed to the farmers of Canada, for members of the opposition continually to go around the country attempting to perpetuate that myth.
So far as the proposals in connection with the agricultural stabilization fund are concerned, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) has made it very clear-and the hon. member has confirmed this tonight- that he wants to have a thorough discussion of this question and he is willing to make adjustments in the proposals before drafting the legislation that is to follow, in order to put whatever the consensus is into effect. At the congress which is to be held here next week there will be ample opportunity to discuss the proposals in the task force report. Indeed, that is what the meeting is for. I am sure the hon. member would be the first to get up in this House and criticize me for determining, in advance of that meeting, what the government will and what it will not accept in respect of the task force recommendations.
I see my time is about up, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion I wish to say it is absolutely wrong to contend that the government is attempting to do away with the family farm, or for that matter rural Canada. We have taken many measures, not to weaken that sector but rather to strengthen it and that is what this government, in particular the Department of Agriculture, is dedicated to do.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.25 p.m.
